## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

PGlite - the WASM build of Postgres from Electric.
Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

## Impact

This is a brand new project. It will establish the foundational architecture including the Node.js backend setup, the embedded PGLite database structure, the SSE connection handling, and the frontend web UI.

PGlite - the WASM build of Postgres from Electric.
Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. Please ensure any contributions that touch code are accompanied by a changeset. ## Acknowledgments PGlite builds on the work of [Stas Kelvich](https://github.com/kelvich) of [Neon](https://neon.tech) in this [Postgres fork](https://github.com/electric-sql/postgres-pglite). ## License PGlite is dual-licensed under the terms of the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/LICENSE) and the [PostgreSQL License](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/POSTGRES-LICENSE), you can choose which you prefer. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

## Impact

This is a brand new project. It will establish the foundational architecture including the Node.js backend setup, the embedded PGLite database structure, the SSE connection handling, and the frontend web UI.

PGlite - the WASM build of Postgres from Electric.
Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities

PGlite - the WASM build of Postgres from Electric.
Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. Please ensure any contributions that touch code are accompanied by a changeset. ## Acknowledgments PGlite builds on the work of [Stas Kelvich](https://github.com/kelvich) of [Neon](https://neon.tech) in this [Postgres fork](https://github.com/electric-sql/postgres-pglite). ## License PGlite is dual-licensed under the terms of the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/LICENSE) and the [PostgreSQL License](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/POSTGRES-LICENSE), you can choose which you prefer. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

## Impact

This is a brand new project. It will establish the foundational architecture including the Node.js backend setup, the embedded PGLite database structure, the SSE connection handling, and the frontend web UI.

PGlite - the WASM build of Postgres from Electric.
Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

## Impact

This is a brand new project. It will establish the foundational architecture including the Node.js backend setup, the embedded PGLite database structure, the SSE connection handling, and the frontend web UI.

PGlite - the WASM build of Postgres from Electric.
Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. Please ensure any contributions that touch code are accompanied by a changeset. ## Acknowledgments PGlite builds on the work of [Stas Kelvich](https://github.com/kelvich) of [Neon](https://neon.tech) in this [Postgres fork](https://github.com/electric-sql/postgres-pglite). ## License PGlite is dual-licensed under the terms of the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/LICENSE) and the [PostgreSQL License](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/POSTGRES-LICENSE), you can choose which you prefer. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

## Impact

This is a brand new project. It will establish the foundational architecture including the Node.js backend setup, the embedded PGLite database structure, the SSE connection handling, and the frontend web UI.

It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. Please ensure any contributions that touch code are accompanied by a changeset. ## Acknowledgments PGlite builds on the work of [Stas Kelvich](https://github.com/kelvich) of [Neon](https://neon.tech) in this [Postgres fork](https://github.com/electric-sql/postgres-pglite). ## License PGlite is dual-licensed under the terms of the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/LICENSE) and the [PostgreSQL License](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/POSTGRES-LICENSE), you can choose which you prefer. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

## Impact

This is a brand new project. It will establish the foundational architecture including the Node.js backend setup, the embedded PGLite database structure, the SSE connection handling, and the frontend web UI.

Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.

- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

PGlite - the WASM build of Postgres from Electric.
Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. Please ensure any contributions that touch code are accompanied by a changeset. ## Acknowledgments PGlite builds on the work of [Stas Kelvich](https://github.com/kelvich) of [Neon](https://neon.tech) in this [Postgres fork](https://github.com/electric-sql/postgres-pglite). ## License PGlite is dual-licensed under the terms of the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/LICENSE) and the [PostgreSQL License](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/POSTGRES-LICENSE), you can choose which you prefer. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

## Impact

This is a brand new project. It will establish the foundational architecture including the Node.js backend setup, the embedded PGLite database structure, the SSE connection handling, and the frontend web UI.

$ cd backend && npm view @electric-sql/pglite readme --no-fund [exit 0] STDOUT:

PGlite - the WASM build of Postgres from Electric.
Build reactive, realtime, local-first apps directly on Postgres.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. This command will: 1. Use Docker to build the Postgres WASM module. The artifacts from this are then copied to `/packages/pglite/release`. 2. Build the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. To _only_ build the Postgres WASM module (i.e. point 1 above), run ```bash pnpm wasm:build ``` If you don't want to build the WASM module and assorted WASM binaries from scratch, you can download them from a comment under the most recently merged PR, labeled as _interim build files_, and place them under `packages/pglite/release`. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. Or alternatively to build a single package, move into the package directory and run: ```bash cd packages/pglite pnpm build ``` When ready to open a PR, run the following command at the root of the repository: ```bash pnpm changeset ``` And follow the instructions to create an appropriate changeset. Please ensure any contributions that touch code are accompanied by a changeset. ## Acknowledgments PGlite builds on the work of [Stas Kelvich](https://github.com/kelvich) of [Neon](https://neon.tech) in this [Postgres fork](https://github.com/electric-sql/postgres-pglite). ## License PGlite is dual-licensed under the terms of the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/LICENSE) and the [PostgreSQL License](https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite/blob/main/POSTGRES-LICENSE), you can choose which you prefer. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
None (Greenfield project).

## Impact

This is a brand new project. It will establish the foundational architecture including the Node.js backend setup, the embedded PGLite database structure, the SSE connection handling, and the frontend web UI.

# PGlite - Postgres in WASM ![PGlite](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/pglite/main/screenshot.png) PGlite is a WASM Postgres build packaged into a TypeScript client library that enables you to run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies. It is only 3mb gzipped and has support for many Postgres extensions, including [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) and [PostGIS](https://postgis.net). ```javascript import { PGlite } from '@electric-sql/pglite' const db = new PGlite() await db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;") // -> { rows: [ { message: "Hello world" } ] } ``` It can be used as an ephemeral in-memory database, or with persistence either to the file system (Node/Bun/Deno) or indexedDB (Browser). Unlike previous "Postgres in the browser" projects, PGlite does not use a Linux virtual machine - it is simply Postgres in WASM. For full documentation and user guides ...[truncated 1381 chars]... , and operates strictly in a single-process mode. As a result, PostgreSQL cannot be directly compiled to WASM for conventional operation. Fortunately, PostgreSQL includes a "single user mode" primarily intended for command-line usage during bootstrapping and recovery procedures. Building upon this capability, PGlite introduces a input/output pathway that facilitates interaction with PostgreSQL when it is compiled to WASM within a JavaScript environment. ## Limitations - PGlite is single user/connection. ## How to build PGlite and contribute The build process of PGlite is split into two parts: 1. Building the Postgres WASM module. 2. Building the PGlite client library and other TypeScript packages. Docker is required to build the WASM module, along with Node (v20 or above) and [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) for package management and building the TypeScript packages. To start checkout the repository and install dependencies: ```bash git clone https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite cd pglite pnpm install ``` To build everything, we have the convenient `pnpm build:all` command in the root of the repository. To build all TypeScript packages (i.e. point 2 of the above), run: ```bash pnpm ts:build ``` This will build all packages in the correct order based on their dependency relationships. You can now develop any individual package using the `build` and `test` scripts, as well as the `stylecheck` and `typecheck` scripts to ensure style and type validity. ## Context

We are building a traditional client-server web application with real-time capabilities. To minimize external dependencies while retaining the power of PostgreSQL, we are using PGLite embedded within a Node.js server. Real-time updates will be pushed to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Provide a simple message board where users can post text messages.
- Ensure all connected clients receive updates instantly when new messages are posted.
- Store data persistently on the local disk using PGLite.
- Keep the frontend incredibly simple and lightweight.

**Non-Goals:**
- User authentication and authorization.
- Rich text formatting or media attachments.
- Horizontal scaling across multiple server instances (PGLite is tied to the single Node instance).

## Decisions

**Decision 1: Embedded PGLite vs External Postgres**
- *Rationale*: PGLite allows us to run PostgreSQL directly inside the Node.js process. This means users don't need to install or configure a separate database service. It seamlessly handles raw SQL queries and can persist to the filesystem.

**Decision 2: Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs WebSockets**
- *Rationale*: We only need one-way real-time communication (Server pushing new messages to Clients). Clients can post new messages via standard HTTP POST requests. SSE is much simpler to implement, works natively over standard HTTP, and doesn't require a complex WebSocket library like Socket.io.

**Decision 3: Vanilla JS / Vite vs React**
- *Rationale*: Given the minimal UI requirements (a message list and a text input), Vanilla JS keeps the build extremely fast and the dependency tree small. Vite provides a great developer experience out of the box.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] PGLite performance on very large datasets: Embedded WASM databases are incredibly fast but might struggle if the dataset grows to tens of gigabytes.
  - *Mitigation*: This is a local application and we expect message volume to be manageable for a single server instance.
- [Risk] SSE connection limits: Browsers have limits on the number of concurrent SSE connections per domain.
  - *Mitigation*: We only need one SSE connection per client tab, which is well within browser limits.

## Why

We need a fast, local-first collaborative message board that allows users to post messages and see updates in real-time. This provides an incredibly low-latency experience by keeping data local while ensuring all users see the same state instantly. It serves as an excellent demonstration of using embedded PGLite combined with Server-Sent Events (SSE) to create a robust, lightweight realtime application without external database dependencies.

## What Changes

- We are introducing a brand new traditional client-server web application.
- The backend will be a Node.js server using an embedded PGLite database for raw SQL queries, persisting data to the local disk.
- Real-time synchronization will be handled via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
- The frontend will be a simple, lightweight Single Page Application (Vanilla JS or React via Vite).

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `realtime-board`: The core message board capability covering posting messages, viewing a message feed, and receiving live updates via SSE.

### Modified Capabilities
